Share SOC 2 + network diagram and KMS doc
Schedule a 2-week benchmark pilot (Redwood to run load test) - target week of 2026-12-28
Follow-up security deep dive with Priya and Redwood security on 2026-12-22
action_items: Maya Chen: Send pricing/commit options and SOW draft - due 2026-12-20
Owen Patel: Prepare benchmark plan and initial capacity recommendation (GPU types, sizing, expected throughput) - due 2026-12-21

summary: Discovery with Sierra Capital about Dedicated capacity. Key needs: reserved GPUs for inference isolation, predictable throughput for low-latency customer-facing LLM features, burst strategy for traffic spikes, and compliance requirements (SOC2, KMS, SSO). Redwood AE + SE to send pricing/SOW and run benchmark pilot. Security deep dive next week.
topics: Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining - this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with me is Owen our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Tom Becker: Doing well, thanks Maya. Tom here, CTO at Sierra.
[00:12] Aisha Rahman: Hi, Aisha Rahman, Head of ML. Excited to dig in.
[00:15] Priya Sharma: Hi all, Priya from DevOps/security.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Awesome. The agenda for today is a Dedicated capacity discovery - we want to understand your latency targets, throughput, isolation needs, and any compliance constraints. We'll also do a quick recommend on GPU sizing and a next step to run a benchmark. Sound good?
[00:30] Tom Becker: Yep, that's the goal. We're evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs a private setup, but leaning Dedicated for predictability and data isolation.
[00:38] Owen Patel: Quick note: when you say Dedicated, do you mean reserved GPU pools with single-tenant isolation, or are you thinking VPC/private control plane?
[00:45] Tom Becker: We want reserved GPUs in our cloud tenancy - single-tenant from a runtime perspective. We still want Redwood to manage the control plane but prefer the compute to be dedicated, ideally in our AWS account.
[00:55] Aisha Rahman: To add, our use cases are twofold: customer-facing chat for financial advisors (low latency, 200 qps at peak) and nightly batch embeddings for analytics (higher throughput but can be batched). Latency target for chat is p95 < 350ms for short prompts (~256 tokens).
[01:12] Maya Chen: Good, that's helpful. For the chat flow, are you using retriever augmentation/hybrid search that will add vector DB latency on top?
[01:18] Aisha Rahman: Yes, we'll have a vector store in front - currently using Pinecone for retrieval. So end-to-end will include retrieval + model inference.
[01:25] Priya Sharma: Our security asks: SOC2 compliance, customer-managed KMS for keys, audit logs retention 1 year, SSO via SAML, RBAC controls, and we need network diagrams for architecture review. Also concerned about data residency for EU customers.
[01:39] Owen Patel: We cover SOC2 and have integrations with KMS/HSM. For Dedicated in a customer VPC we can support customer-managed keys via KMS. Audit logs and per-request tracing are available in Redwood Console.
[01:48] Tom Becker: What's the typical Dedicated sizing you recommend for a profile like ours? 200 qps peak with 256 token responses.
[01:55] Owen Patel: Roughly speaking, for 200 qps at 256 tokens with a 7-13B model, you'd be looking at multi-GPU racks - perhaps 4-8 A100s if you're aiming for strict low-latency p95. If you go with quantized LLM variants or a 30B optimized model the numbers shift. We usually recommend starting with a baseline cluster and a burst pool.
[02:10] Aisha Rahman: Are those A100s or AMD MI250s? We're evaluating costs.
[02:14] Owen Patel: We showed A100 as an example; we support multiple hardware types - A100, H100, and we can run on MI250 in some cloud regions. Cost and latency differ. We'll include cost tradeoffs in the pricing deck.
[02:23] Maya Chen: Aisha, when you say burst pool, do you mean an on-demand capacity that can scale quickly for spikes?
[02:29] Aisha Rahman: Exactly. We'll have diurnal spikes and occasional product launches that 5x normal traffic for hours. We need a predictable plan to handle that without losing p95.
[02:37] Owen Patel: We support a hybrid model: reserved baseline (Dedicated committed GPUs) plus a burst tier that can be on-demand or reserved-but-idle at lower cost. Burst can be served from either Redwood Hosted spare capacity or additional customer-managed nodes that are cold until needed.
[02:50] Priya Sharma: If burst uses hosted capacity, what about data residency and isolation during those bursts? We can't have EU traffic leave region or be processed on shared tenants for regulated customers.
[02:59] Owen Patel: Good question. For region/residency constraints we can route bursts to dedicated spare capacity in the same region; we also offer circuit-breaker policies so certain tenants never use shared hosts. We'll capture these policies in the SOW.
[03:12] Tom Becker: What about autoscaling times? We need capacity scaled in under 2 minutes for chat spikes.
[03:17] Owen Patel: Autoscaling cold-starting GPUs will take time - boot, load model, warm KV cache. To meet 2-minute SLOs we typically keep a small warm pool of standby instances with the model(s) loaded and ready; that reduces scale time significantly. We'll size that standby pool based on observed spike frequency.
[03:31] Aisha Rahman: That standby idea makes sense. How do you handle KV cache warm-up? For chats heavy on context window caching, warming KV cache is key to latencies.
[03:40] Owen Patel: We do prefix/KV caching and can pre-populate caches for known prompts or keep long-lived sessions pinned to specific workers. For Dedicated deployments we can tune the KV cache retention more aggressively. There's a tradeoff with memory.
[03:50] Tom Becker: On security, we need to ensure that logs are sent to our SIEM and that we can revoke access quickly. Also, audit logs must show per-token request IDs.
[04:00] Maya Chen: Redwood's audit logs include request IDs, model versions, and metadata; we can forward to Splunk/Datadog or your SIEM. Access controls include RBAC and SSO.
[04:06] Priya Sharma: Do you offer encryption-in-use or only at-rest and transit?
[04:11] Owen Patel: We support encryption at rest (customer KMS) and in transit. For encryption-in-use, we can integrate with HSM-based workflows for key operations but full HE/TEE is not standard; we can discuss threat models in the security deep dive.
[04:24] Aisha Rahman: For the nightly batch embeddings, what throughput should we expect vs cost? Will batching and quantization help reduce GPU needs significantly?
[04:33] Owen Patel: Yes - embeddings batch well. You can sequentialize thousands of items and use INT8 or Q4 quantization to reduce memory and increase throughput. That batch job can often run on cheaper GPU types or even CPU for small models; we'll advise per-workload.
[04:45] Tom Becker: Pricing: we want committed pricing tiers - e.g., 4/8/16 GPU commits and overage rates.
[04:51] Maya Chen: We'll send a Dedicated pricing deck with commit options and overage rules. The SOW will outline burst policies and SLAs.
[04:57] Priya Sharma: One more question on network: We need details for firewall rules, VIPs, and whether we need private link or VPN.
[05:05] Owen Patel: For customer-managed VPC we often use private link for control plane communication and VPC peering for data plane; we will provide a network diagram and the exact ports. We'll include options for VPN or Direct Connect.
[05:16] Aisha Rahman: Any caveats with model rollouts? We want canary and automatic rollback, plus the ability to pin model versions per route.
[05:24] Owen Patel: Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B routing, automatic fallback to previous model variants on error. You can pin routes to model versions in the Console or via API. We also keep model-level metrics and quality regression alerts tied to evals.
[05:36] Tom Becker: How do we validate cost vs latency at scale? Can Redwood run a benchmark against our traffic shape?
[05:42] Owen Patel: Yes - we propose a 2-week benchmark pilot: you provide representative prompts and traffic shape, we run load tests in Dedicated cluster with telemetry so you can validate p95/p99 and cost per token.
[05:51] Maya Chen: For the pilot we'd need sample prompts, typical session lengths, and a list of model variants you want tested. Owen will draft a benchmark plan.
[05:59] Aisha Rahman: Okay. Also, we have a compliance list for EU customer data and some customers in PCI scope - will Dedicated cover PCI workloads?
[06:09] Priya Sharma: Specifically, payment card data touches chat transcripts for advisors, so we need guidance.
[06:13] Owen Patel: PCI is sensitive; we can support PCI workloads with an on-prem Private deployment or with strict isolation and controls in Dedicated plus customer-managed KMS and hardened audit controls. We'll flag that for the security deep dive.
[06:25] Tom Becker: What's the expected turnaround for the security package? We want SOC2 report, pen test summary, network diagram.
[06:31] Maya Chen: We can share SOC2 and high-level pen test artifacts within 24-48 hours; the VPC/network diagram and KMS integration guide we'll attach to the SOW.
[06:38] Priya Sharma: We also need information on key rotation and access revocation - how fast can keys be rotated and access removed?
[06:44] Owen Patel: With customer-managed KMS you control key rotation and revocation. For user-level access via SSO we can map SAML group changes to RBAC in minutes, but full session revocation is a function of token TTLs; we'll show the configuration options.
[06:56] Tom Becker: On the operations side, what's the expected life-cycle for model upgrades? We want a rollback window and baseline performance tests before rollout.
[07:05] Owen Patel: We support staged rollouts with canary gates; you can run synthetic evals and compare output quality and latency before promoting. Automatic rollback triggers can be configured on latency or error thresholds.
[07:15] Aisha Rahman: For local ML engineers, what APIs/SDKs are available? We'll want a Python SDK for calls and an internal metrics plugin.
[07:21] Maya Chen: We have REST + official Python and Node SDKs; we also expose streaming responses and function calling. Telemetry hooks are available to forward traces to your tracing backend.
[07:30] Priya Sharma: Any issues with compliance when using third-party retrieval (e.g., Pinecone)? We might need to ensure vectors are stored in region and masked.
[07:37] Owen Patel: That's typically handled on the retrieval side - you can configure Pinecone to use specific regions and set TTLs or tokenization strategies. For highly regulated content we recommend avoiding third-party vector stores or using private instances.
[07:37] Maya Chen: Ok I want to quickly recap the key constraints: 1) p95 < 350ms for chat, 2) 200 qps peak, 3) bursts up to 5x, 4) SOC2/KMS/SSO and PCI considerations, 5) EU data residency. We'll follow up with pricing/SOW and a benchmark plan.
[08:00] Tom Becker: Sounds good. Anything else on your side?
[08:05] Priya Sharma: We'll share a network diagram and our compliance checklist by Friday.
[08:09] Aisha Rahman: We'll also put together a representative prompt corpus for the benchmark.
[08:13] Maya Chen: Great. Owen, you'll own the benchmark plan?
[08:16] Owen Patel: Yep, I'll draft it and include test scenarios for chat latency, embedding throughput, and cold-start burst behavior.
[08:22] Maya Chen: Last question from me - any blockers for running the pilot in the week of Dec 28?
[08:26] Aisha Rahman: No blockers as long as we can sign an MSA and the SOW for the pilot.
[08:31] Tom Becker: We'll expedite legal if possible.
[08:34] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll send the pricing deck, SOW draft, SOC2 docs and the benchmark plan. Follow-up call for security deep dive scheduled for 2026-12-22. Thanks everyone.
[08:45] Tom Becker: Thanks all.
[08:47] Priya Sharma: Thanks.
[08:48] Aisha Rahman: Thank you.
[08:50] Maya Chen: Bye everyone.
